content:
Quick answer: Living with arthritis pain, flares and uncertainty commonly affects mood, and low mood or worry can make pain feel worse. Talk to your GP, or self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies in England, if low mood or anxiety lasts more than two weeks. Paced movement, sleep, social contact and realistic goals help. If you feel unsafe, call 999 or Samaritans on 116 123.

Arthritis is not only about joints. Pain that comes and goes, giving up things you love, money or work worries, and feeling misunderstood can all wear you down. Depression and anxiety are more common in people with long-term painful conditions, and NICE has specific guidance for depression alongside a long-term physical health problem. Feeling this way is not weakness — it is a recognised part of living with a long-term condition, and help is available.

If you feel unsafe right now: call 999 or go to A&E. You can call Samaritans free, any time, on 116 123, or call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option.

How pain and mood affect each other

  • Pain and poor sleep drain energy and patience — see our sleeping with arthritis guide
  • Loss of roles — work, hobbies, caring or getting out can shrink
  • Uncertainty — not knowing how tomorrow's joints will feel
  • Fatigue — which can look like, and overlap with, low mood (read our arthritis fatigue guide)
  • Isolation — doing less socially because of pain or flares

Low mood can then make pain feel louder and movement harder, which is why looking after both together usually works best.

Signs it is worth talking to someone

  • Feeling low, hopeless or tearful most days for two weeks or more
  • Losing interest in things you usually enjoy
  • Constant worry, panic, or avoiding activity out of fear of pain
  • Sleeping much more or much less, or changes in appetite
  • Thoughts that you would be better off not here — get help the same day

NHS and UK support

  • Your GP — you can talk about mood as well as joints; it is a normal part of reviewing a long-term condition
  • NHS Talking Therapies — in England you can usually self-refer online without seeing your GP first; Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own routes through your GP
  • Pain management programmes — ask your GP or rheumatology team; they combine movement, pacing and psychological skills
  • Your rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist — tell them if fear of pain is stopping you moving
  • Carers — family who support you can ask for a carer's assessment for their own wellbeing

Things that often help day to day

  1. Paced movement — short, regular activity from the exercise hub or a walking plan can lift mood as well as joints
  2. Pacing — fewer boom-and-bust days means fewer crashes; see pacing and energy management
  3. A flare plan — knowing what you will do takes some of the fear out of flares; use our flare action plan
  4. Stay connected — one call, message or short visit a day counts
  5. Reduce money and work stress — check the Benefits & PIP hub and arthritis at work guide

Our longer arthritis and mental health hub has more on coping with diagnosis, flares and relationships. If you have just been diagnosed, the newly diagnosed guide can help you feel more in control.

Frequently asked questions

Will antidepressants affect my arthritis medicines?

Some medicines interact, so your GP or pharmacist will check your full list. Never stop or start a medicine without advice.

Is it all in my head?

No. Pain is real. Psychological support helps because the brain and nervous system process pain, not because the pain is imaginary.

Can this chat or website support me in a crisis?

No. We provide education only. In a crisis call 999, Samaritans on 116 123, or NHS 111.
